The Mongol conquest of Cumania was the 13th-century conquest of the Cuman–Kipchak confederation by the Mongol Empire. Following the Mongol victory at the Battle of the Kalka River in 1223, a larger campaign under Batu Khan (1236–1241) brought the Pontic–Caspian steppe under Mongol control. The territory was incorporated into the ulus of Jochi, later known as the Golden Horde, and many Cumans fled westward into Hungary.
Background
In the 11th century, the Cuman–Kipchaks occupied the steppes of present-day Kazakhstan and gradually expanded into the forested steppe of south-western Siberia and the southern Urals, pushing northern forest peoples further north or assimilating those who remained in their territories. By the 13th century, the Kipchak steppe and south-western Siberia were overrun by the Mongols and incorporated into the khanate later known as the Golden Horde under Batu.
Conquest
As Mongol forces advanced across southern Russia, large numbers of Cumans and Kipchaks fled westward into Poland and Hungary to escape the invasion. While some Cuman groups submitted to Mongol authority, the Cuman leader Köten fled with approximately 40,000 followers and sought refuge in Hungary. King Béla IV, who had ascended the throne in 1235, admitted the Cumans into his kingdom. Hungary possessed a powerful cavalry force, and the Cuman horsemen were regarded as a potential military reinforcement against the advancing Mongols.
The first Mongol expeditions crossed into Cuman territory in 1222–1224, led by generals Jebe and Subutai. These campaigns targeted multiple Cuman tribes, including the Barli, which caused widespread forced displacements of Cuman populations toward southeastern Europe. Further campaigns occurred in 1228–1229 and culminated in the massive westward offensive under Batu Khan in 1236, which destroyed Volga Bulgaria and then advanced into the western Dasht-i Kipchak. During this period, notable battles included the siege of Sodak and the subjugation of Cuman groups who resisted Mongol authority.
Aftermath
The Mongol conquest devastated the Cuman confederation. Many Cuman nobles were killed or captured, including the khan Köten's relatives, while surviving populations fled to Hungary, the Balkans, and other neighboring regions. The conquest also disrupted the ethnic composition of the steppe and facilitated the eventual replacement of the term 'Kipchak' with 'Tatar' in the Golden Horde territories. The disruption of Cuman society allowed the Mongols to establish military outposts and secure control over key strategic areas along the Danube and Black Sea coasts.
